name: The Dilbert Principle
statement: Companies tend to promote their least-competent employees to management, to limit the damage they can do.
statementAccent: to limit the damage they can do
meaning: A satirical inversion of merit-based promotion: rather than advancing the capable, organisations move their worst performers up into management — where, in the joke's logic, they are farthest from real production and can break the least.
mechanism: Promotion works as containment rather than reward: the incompetent are relocated to where they can do least harm — into management, away from the 'real work' — without the friction of firing them. Dogbert's version in the strip: 'Leadership is nature's way of removing morons from the productive flow.'

examples.text: The core gag: an employee too inept to be trusted with engineering or production gets a management title. The humour is that the organisation rationalises damage-limitation as advancement.

In a functioning organisation, promotion ideally tracks demonstrated capability and adds coordination value. The Dilbert principle is the cynical mirror image, where the promotion channel is used to offload liability — and the gap between the two is the joke.

variants.name: The Peter principle
variants.text: The serious cousin, and the key contrast: under the Peter principle people are promoted for past competence until they reach a job they cannot do; under the Dilbert principle the already-incompetent are promoted precisely to sideline them. Incompetence is an endpoint in one, an entry criterion in the other.

variants.name: Putt's law
variants.text: The R&D-management version of the same negative selection: those who understand do not manage, and those who manage do not understand.

whyItMatters: It is the sharpest comic statement of a real anxiety — that organisations sometimes promote to remove people from where they matter, not to reward them — and it gave a generation of office workers a name for it. Its value is as satire that lands, not as a finding.

working.lead: Don't use promotion as a dumping ground
working.text: the principle bites when moving a poor performer 'up and out of the way' is easier than managing or replacing them; that convenience is the trap.

working.lead: Keep it distinct from the Peter principle
working.text: diagnosing which you are seeing matters — one is failure of a merit rule, the other is a deliberate sidelining with no merit logic at all.

limits: It is satire, not an empirical finding — Scott Adams is a cartoonist, not an organisational researcher, and offered no data. It is a cynical overgeneralisation, funny because it exaggerates; plenty of organisations promote capable people who thrive. And unlike the Peter principle, which at least posits a plausible pseudo-mechanism, the Dilbert principle assumes a deliberate, self-aware sidelining that real firms rarely execute as described.
misreadings: It is a joke, not a management theory — it does not claim firms literally select for incompetence in a measurable way. Read straight it is false; read as satire it captures a real fear about how promotion can be misused.
origin: Coined by Scott Adams, creator of the Dilbert comic strip, in a 1995 Wall Street Journal article titled 'The Dilbert Principle' and expanded into his 1996 bestselling book of the same name. Adams meant it satirically, as workplace comedy drawn from corporate life, and framed it explicitly as a riff on the Peter principle.

sources.text: Adams, S. (1996). The Dilbert Principle. HarperBusiness. — the book expanding the 1995 Wall Street Journal article.
